Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
cut off all contact with friends and family

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette:
Marcus Ellison is a 51-year-old widowed school principal who presented for psychological assessment following what he described, with visible difficulty, as "the year that took everything from me." He is a tall, measured man who chose his words carefully during intake, occasionally pausing mid-sentence as though testing the ground before stepping onto it. He came to the first session in his work clothes, having driven directly from school, and mentioned almost immediately that he had not told any of his staff why he had this appointment.

Approximately fourteen months before seeking help, Marcus was diagnosed with bacterial endocarditis following what he had initially dismissed as fatigue and a low-grade fever. He had delayed seeking medical attention for several weeks, attributing his symptoms to grief - his wife, Denise, had died of ovarian cancer eighteen months prior, and he had grown accustomed to feeling hollowed out. When he finally presented to the emergency department, his condition had deteriorated significantly. He was admitted to the ICU, where he spent eleven days. He has fragmented recollections of that period: the antiseptic cold of the air, the sharp medicinal smell that seemed to saturate everything, the IV lines taped to his arm, a cardiologist speaking to him in a tone that Marcus understood, even through the fog, meant that the situation was serious. At one point, a nurse administered an alcohol swab to his inner arm before a procedure, and the smell - clean, clinical, slightly sweet - preceded a moment in which he was told there was a real possibility he would not survive without emergency intervention.

He recovered physically. What did not recover, or at least did not return to anything he recognised, was his sense of himself.

In the months that followed discharge, Marcus found that certain things undid him without warning. Walking past the school nurse's office one afternoon, he caught a trace of antiseptic from inside the room, and before he could locate the thought, his body had already responded - his chest tightened, his arms felt heavy and positioned as though lying flat, and he was flooded with an emotion he could not attach to any clear image, only to a terrible certainty that something was ending. The smell of alcohol - hand sanitiser in the school foyer, a colleague's breath at a Friday gathering - produced a similar collapse. He began to feel that his body was not a reliable narrator of the present moment; it seemed to speak only in the language of that hospital room, regardless of where he actually was.

He had come to believe, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that his body could betray him again at any time and without warning. This belief had reorganised much of his daily life. He had cancelled two routine medical appointments and had not rescheduled them. When his GP's office called to follow up on post-discharge bloodwork, he let the calls go to voicemail. He understood, in some rational register, that this was not sensible behaviour for a man with his history, but the prospect of a medical examination - the smell of the room, the positioning on a table, the clinical attention paid to his chest - felt not like precaution but like rehearsal for catastrophe.

He had also, gradually and then completely, stopped seeing friends. He rehearsed conversations before any interaction, scripting responses to questions he anticipated - about his health, about how he was managing - because he was certain that if he did not control the exchange, something would come undone in front of someone. Over the course of six months, the rehearsals became exhausting enough that he stopped initiating contact altogether. Several close friendships, some dating back to his years as a classroom teacher, had quietly lapsed. His daughter had called twice in the past month without a reply.

When he tried to deliberately recall what had happened in the ICU, he found he could not access it in any coherent way - the sequence refused to assemble itself. Yet the emotional weight of it arrived without invitation, attached to nothing he could name or examine.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment in his own school hallway. A student had used hand sanitiser nearby, and Marcus had to excuse himself to his office, close the door, and sit on the floor for several minutes with his arms pressed flat against his sides, waiting for his body to believe it was somewhere else. He told the intake clinician that he no longer recognised the person who had done that. What he most feared, he said, was that this was now simply who he was. What he most hoped, though he said it as though he barely believed it, was that it wasn't.
